name: Khmu
catalog_quote: In Khmu a phonological word may be defined as a phonological stretch containing only one main (stressed) syllable. It may be preceded by one unstressed or, very rarely, two unstressed syllables. Thus in this language where the stress is fixed, stress can be used for defining the word. [...] There are two types of syllables in Khmu words: main syllables and presyllables. A main syllable is the syl…
sweep_summary: Khmu (khmu1256) is in the catalog as fixed-strict (final/main-syllable stress, WORD domain, no lexical stress), deciding source Premsrirat 1987 A Khmu Grammar p.5. Both sweep items are Glottolog false positives: the reference pages for 408084 (Wenk 1987, speech rhythm in music) and 604049 (Carlson & Tyler 2018, English pitch accents and attachment) each state the Khmu lgcode is a 'computerized assignment from \"just\"'; neither concerns Khmu (Carlson & Tyler confirmed English-only via its open PMC copy)..., quote verbatim), Suwilai 1999 MKS 29 ('A word has only one strong stress, which is always on the last syllable'), Cooper & Cooper 2001 MKS (PW = (Sr)+Sm, fully stressed main syllable), Svantesson & Karlsson 2004 TAL (stressed major syllable preceded by unstressed minor syllable), and House et al. 2009 Interspeech (fetched sources; phrase-final accent only, silent on word stress). All four first-hand statements confirm the catalog coding; nothing contradicts or refines it. Unread leads: Svantesson 1983 Kammu phonology and morphology (print only, medium priority), Svantesson & House 2006 Phonology and Karlsson et al. 2012 Phonetica (tone/intonation, paywalled, low priority).

new_statements.quote: The Khmu syllable structure comprises one or more consonants and a vowel and may be of two types, unstressed presyllable and stressed main syllable. The main syllable canon is 'C(C)V(C). A phonological word in Khmu may have one, two, or three syllables. A word has only one strong stress, which is always on the last syllable.

new_statements.locator: §1 'Word and syllable structures', p.57 (scanned p-01, lines 66-73)
new_statements.reading: Fixed word-final stress across five Khmu dialects of Nan and Chiengrai: one strong stress per word, always on the last (main) syllable; presyllables are unstressed and reducible. Confirms the catalog's fixed-strict, WORD-domain, no-lexical-stress coding. The catalog's deciding source (Premsrirat 1987, A Khmu Grammar, PL A-75, §2.1-2.2 p.5) was re-read from the copied PDF and its quote is verbatim; the 1999 paper is a second first-hand statement by the same author and is the crispest wording of the position ('always on the last syllable').

audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-strict, final/main-syllable stress, domain WORD) rests on Premsrirat 1987, a full descriptive grammar with an explicit Stress section, held as open-access PDF+txt; both deciding passages (p.5 and p.24) are verbatim in the held text. Three further open sources fetched sources now (Premsrirat 1999 MKS 29; Cooper & Cooper 2001 SEALS IX; Svantesson & Karlsson 2004 TAL) independently state one stressed main/major syllable, word-final, preceded by unstressed presyllable(s) — all confirm. The one unheld work that could count as 'better for phonology' (Svantesson 1983, print-only) is by an author whose later open paper states the same pattern, so no recode risk. sources.quote: The Khmu syllable structure comprises one or more consonants and a vowel and may be of two types, unstressed presyllable and stressed main syllable. The main syllable canon is 'C(C)V(C). A phonological word in Khmu may have one, two, or three syllables. A word has only one strong stress, which is always on the last syllable.
sources.locator: §1 'Word and syllable structures', p.57 (scanned p-01, lines 66-73)
sources.note: Five Khmu dialects of Nan and Chiengrai: syllables are unstressed presyllables or stressed main syllables; a phonological word has 1-3 syllables and exactly one strong stress, always on the last syllable; presyllables are unstressed and may be reduced or deleted across dialects. Confirms fixed final (main-syllable) stress; no lexical contrast.

sources.citation: Cooper, Michael & Susan Cooper 2001. A preliminary phonological analysis of Huay Jo Khmu. In Papers from the Ninth Annual Meeting of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society, 51-72. Tempe: Arizona State University.
sources.quote: 'The phonological word in Khmu Kroong is the domain of the minimal stress contour ... PW = (Sr)+Sm. The phonological word (PW) consists of a main (fully stressed) syllable (Sm) optionally preceded by a reduced (weakly stressed) syllable (Sr). Thus, in general, phonological words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic.'

sources.citation: Suwilai Premsrirat (1987). A Khmu Grammar. In Suwilai Premsrirat (ed.), Papers in South-East Asian Linguistics No. 10: Khmu, a minority language of Thailand, Pacific Linguistics A-75:1-144. Canberra: ANU.
sources.quote: In Khmu a phonological word may be defined as a phonological stretch containing only one main (stressed) syllable. It may be preceded by one unstressed or, very rarely, two unstressed syllables. Thus in this language where the stress is fixed, stress can be used for defining the word. [...] A main syllable is the syllable that occurs alone as a monosyllabic word or as the last syllable of a disyllabic or trisyllabic word. It is always stressed. Its vowel has full quality. The presyllable, the syllable that comes before the main syllable, is always unstressed and very weak.
sources.locator: §2.1-2.2, p.5 (txt lines 343-373; page marker '5' at line 312)
sources.note: Stress is fixed and defines the phonological word: one main (stressed) syllable per word, optionally preceded by one (rarely two) unstressed presyllables; the main syllable is the last syllable of a di-/trisyllabic word and 'is always stressed'; presyllables 'always unstressed and very weak'. Matches catalog quote verbatim (extracted textorder slightly scrambled in §2.1).

sources.quote: 'a sizeable part of the vocabulary of many Mon-Khmer languages consists of sesquisyllabic words which have one stressed major syllable preceded by an unstressed minor syllable' (applied to Northern/Yuan Kammu; minor-syllable nucleus a non-phonemic epenthetic schwa).
sources.note: Northern (Yuan) Kammu of Nam Tha, Laos: sesquisyllabic words have one stressed major syllable preceded by an unstressed minor syllable; the paper's topic is contrastive tone on minor syllables (prosody), but the passing statement confirms fixed stress on the major (final) syllable.

sources.quote: Both dialects seem to engage the phrase-final accent to simultaneously convey focus, phrase finality, utterance finality, and speaker engagement.
sources.note: Phrase-final accent, focus and F0 truncation in tonal vs non-tonal Kammu dialects (scripted speech, 19 speakers). No statement on word-stress placement (grep for stress/major/minor syllable: none).
